title: Module Overview and Imports
content: Three Mathlib imports: `Logic.Function.Basic` (basic function definitions), `Data.Set.Function` (set-theoretic function properties including `Function.Surjective`), and `Tactic` (standard tactics). The module docstring introduces Cantor's 1891 diagonal argument, which proves that no enumeration of infinite binary sequences can be complete — establishing that the reals are uncountable. The proof is entirely original: no non-trivial Mathlib theorems are used for the main result.
mathContext: The file proves $\nexists f : \mathbb{N} \to 2^{\mathbb{N}}$ surjective, and more generally $\nexists f : S \to \mathcal{P}(S)$ surjective for any type $S$. Only basic logic and function definitions from Mathlib are imported.

title: Binary Sequences as Functions
content: A **binary sequence** is modeled as a function from natural numbers to booleans: `BinarySeq := ℕ → Bool`. Each sequence assigns either `true` (1) or `false` (0) to every position. These correspond to real numbers in $[0, 1]$ via binary expansion: the sequence $(b_0, b_1, b_2, \ldots)$ represents $0.b_0 b_1 b_2 \ldots$ in binary. The identification is not quite bijective (e.g., $0.0111\ldots = 0.1000\ldots$) but this minor issue does not affect the uncountability argument.
mathContext: $\text{BinarySeq} := \mathbb{N} \to \text{Bool} \cong 2^{\mathbb{N}}$. The set $2^{\mathbb{N}}$ has the same cardinality as $\mathbb{R}$ (via binary expansion). Example: the sequence $1, 0, 1, 0, \ldots$ represents $0.101010\ldots_2 = 2/3$.

title: The Diagonal Construction
content: Given any enumeration $f : \mathbb{N} \to \text{BinarySeq}$, we construct a **diagonal sequence** by looking at position $n$ of sequence $f(n)$ and flipping that bit. Formally: `diagonal f n := !(f n n)`. This ensures the new sequence differs from $f(n)$ at position $n$ for every $n$. The construction is purely computable — no choice axiom needed.
mathContext: $\text{diagonal}(f)(n) = \neg f(n)(n)$. This is a concrete computable function: given any enumeration, the diagonal is deterministically constructed by bit-flipping along the main diagonal of the infinite matrix $(f(i)(j))_{i,j \in \mathbb{N}}$.

title: Key Lemma: Diagonal Differs at Each Position
content: The heart of the argument: `diagonal f n ≠ f n n` for every $n$. The proof unfolds `diagonal` to get `!(f n n) ≠ f n n`, then uses `cases` on `f n n : Bool` — in both cases (`true` and `false`), `simp` closes the goal since `!true ≠ true` and `!false ≠ false`. This two-line proof captures the entire logical content of Cantor's diagonal argument.

title: Cantor's Diagonalization Theorem
content: **Cantor's Theorem**: For any $f : \mathbb{N} \to \text{BinarySeq}$, there exists a sequence $s$ not in the range of $f$. The proof introduces $f$, witnesses $s = \text{diagonal}(f)$ via `use`, then for each $n$ assumes $f(n) = \text{diagonal}(f)$ for contradiction. The key step: `congrFun h n` extracts pointwise equality $f(n)(n) = \text{diagonal}(f)(n)$, which contradicts `diagonal_differs f n`. This is the standard proof-by-contradiction structure of the diagonal argument.
mathContext: $\forall f : \mathbb{N} \to 2^{\mathbb{N}},\; \exists s \in 2^{\mathbb{N}},\; \forall n,\; f(n) \neq s$. Witness: $s = \text{diagonal}(f)$. For each $n$: if $f(n) = s$, then $f(n)(n) = s(n) = \neg f(n)(n)$, contradiction.

title: No Surjection and Uncountability of Reals
content: `no_surjection_nat_to_binary` reformulates the main theorem as $\neg \exists f, \text{Surjective}(f)$: assume a surjection exists, apply `cantor_diagonalization` to get a sequence not in the range, then derive contradiction with surjectivity. `reals_uncountable` is a direct synonym, emphasizing the set-theoretic interpretation: $|\mathbb{N}| < |\mathbb{R}|$. The identification $\text{BinarySeq} \cong [0,1] \cong \mathbb{R}$ (via binary expansion and a bijection $[0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$) is noted in the docstring but not formalized.
mathContext: $\neg \exists f : \mathbb{N} \to 2^{\mathbb{N}},\; \text{Surjective}(f)$. Equivalently: $|\mathbb{N}| < |2^{\mathbb{N}}| = |\mathbb{R}| = \mathfrak{c}$ (the cardinality of the continuum).

title: Cantor's Power Set Theorem
content: The general version: for **any** type $S$, there is no surjection from $S$ to $\text{Set}\,S$. The proof defines the diagonal set $D = \{x : x \notin f(x)\}$, obtains $a$ with $f(a) = D$ by surjectivity, then derives $a \in D \leftrightarrow a \notin D$ — a contradiction resolved by `by_cases h : a ∈ D`. This is the general form; the binary sequence version follows by taking $S = \mathbb{N}$ and noting $\text{Set}\,\mathbb{N} \cong (\mathbb{N} \to \text{Bool})$.

title: Connection to Russell's Paradox
content:
The diagonal set $D = \{x : x 
otin f(x)\}$ is formally identical to Russell's paradox when $f = 	ext{id}$: it becomes $\{x : x 
otin x\}$, the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. In naive set theory, this leads to a genuine paradox (if $R \in R$ then $R 
otin R$, and vice versa). In type theory (and ZFC), the paradox is avoided by stratification: elements and sets live at different type levels, so $x \in x$ is not well-typed. `diagonal_set_paradox` formalizes the self-referential structure: for any $a$ with $f(a) = D$, we get $a \in D \iff a 
otin D$.

title: Visualization of the Diagonal Argument
content: An ASCII art visualization showing the infinite matrix of binary sequences with the diagonal elements highlighted in brackets. The diagonal extracts $f(0)(0), f(1)(1), f(2)(2), \ldots$ and flipping each bit produces a sequence guaranteed to differ from row $n$ at column $n$. This visual representation makes the self-referential structure of the argument concrete and is the standard pedagogical illustration found in introductory set theory texts.
mathContext: The matrix $(f(i)(j))_{i,j \in \mathbb{N}}$ has diagonal $(f(n)(n))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, and the flipped diagonal $(\neg f(n)(n))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ differs from row $n$ at column $n$ for every $n$.
